Supporting Information

Testing the wind disruption and disturbance refugia hypothesis for mountain pine beetle outbreaks (Dendroctonus ponderosae). Terrain, stand density and flight-period wind as controls on attack in the Selkirk Mountains of British Columbia

Author
Affiliation

Seamus Murphy

TÜV SÜD

Table S1

The datasets the study combined, with the spatial and temporal resolution of each.

Dataset Source Spatial Temporal Extent
Red-stage attack Landsat 5 and 8 Collection 2 Level-2 30 m 1 year and 16 days 8 years and 47 periods
Stand structure Vegetation Resources Inventory, annual releases 30 m, rasterised 1 year 8 snapshots
Terrain Natural Resources Canada High Resolution Digital Elevation Model 30 m static 61,923 cells
Station wind Environment and Climate Change Canada hourly stations 9 stations within 150 km 1 hour 19,157 hours
Terrain-resolved wind MicroMet terrain adjustment of station wind 30 m 1 year and 16 days 8 years and 47 periods
Model tables Rows joined from the above 30 m 1 year and 16 days 64,000 cell-years and 173,086 cell-periods

Table S3

The environmental variables that entered the annual models, grouped by the mechanism each represented. M0 contained host size, shading and landform, M1 added stand density, M2 added terrain exposure to wind, terrain shape and flight-window radiation, and M3 added station wind and the interactions of basal area with the wind shelter index, July wind and flight-window radiation.

Variable Mechanism
Susceptible pine basal area (m² ha⁻¹) Host size
Stand age (years) Host size
Quadratic mean diameter (cm) Host size
Sky view factor Topographic shading
Northness Topographic shading
Elevation (m) Landform
Stand basal area (m² ha⁻¹) Stand density
Wind shelter index Terrain exposure to wind
Topographic position index Terrain shape
Convergence index Terrain shape
Profile curvature Terrain shape
Flight-window direct radiation (kWh/m²) Flight-window radiation
July mean wind (km/h) Station wind
June mean wind (km/h) Station wind
July wind, previous summer (km/h) Station wind, previous summer
June wind, previous summer (km/h) Station wind, previous summer
Surface temperature, previous flight window (°C) Measured surface temperature, previous summer
Ground roughness within the cell at 1 m (m) Terrain at the scale of single trees
Share of the cell facing north at 5 m Terrain at the scale of single trees
Spread of position at 55 m (m) Terrain at the scale of single trees
Crown closure (%) Stand density
Modelled wind at 90 m, previous summer (km/h) Terrain wind model, previous summer
Upslope share of flight hours, previous summer Terrain wind model, previous summer

Table S4

Coefficients of the sixteen-day models. E1 had no dependence terms, E2 added the cell’s own state in the previous period and the share attacked around it, and E3 added the same two terms for the same period of the previous year. Estimates are changes in log-odds per standard deviation, with standard errors, the number of cells and the AUC of each model; intercepts and geomorphon classes are not shown. * p ≤ 0.05, ** p ≤ 0.01, *** p ≤ 0.001, **** p ≤ 0.0001.

Methods S1

The wind component of the MicroMet model of Liston & Elder (2006) is seven equations, implemented directly from the source paper with its equation numbers given below.

Terrain slope \(\beta\) and slope azimuth \(\xi\) came from the elevation model, equations 12 and 13 of Liston & Elder (2006). Curvature \(\Omega_c\) is a cell’s elevation minus the mean of the two opposite cells one curvature length scale away, taken on four direction lines and averaged, their equation 14, and the length scale was estimated as the first lag at which elevation autocorrelation fell below 0.5, which was 600 m here. Assigning \(\theta\) to wind bearing, slope in the wind direction was computed as follows

\[\Omega_s = \beta \cos(\theta - \xi) \tag{1}\]

with \(\Omega_s\) and \(\Omega_c\) each scaled to \([-0.5,\,0.5]\). The terrain weighting factor applied to the observed speed \(W\) was derived using

\[W_w = 1 + \gamma_s \Omega_s + \gamma_c \Omega_c, \qquad \gamma_s = \gamma_c = 0.5 \tag{2}\]

This provided the basis for calculation of the terrain-modified speed using

\[W_t = W_w W \tag{3}\]

and a diversion of wind direction computed as

\[\theta_d = -\tfrac{1}{2}\, \Omega_s \sin\!\left[2(\xi - \theta)\right]. \tag{4}\]

By Equation 2, \(W_w\) depends on direction and not on speed, so it was computed once for each of 16 wind direction sectors of 22.5 degrees, the sixteen points of the compass, and each hourly observation was multiplied by the surface for its own sector, so that nothing was averaged before the terrain acted on it, and over all sectors \(W_w\) ran from 0.66 to 1.32.

Figure S1

The flight window against the landscape’s own climate, from hourly Environment and Climate Change Canada station records for May to September of the study years. The shaded band marked the window, 1 July to 15 August, taken from the bionomics and not fitted to these data. (a) Mean afternoon temperature by day of year, with the 19 to 41 degrees C flight range and the 22 to 32 degrees C peak band marked. (b) The share of afternoon hours inside the flight range, day by day. (c) Mean temperature and the share of all hours inside the flight range, by hour, with the 12:00 to 17:00 restriction shaded. (d) Mean wind speed by hour on the same axis, showing that the hours in which the beetle could fly were also the windiest of the day.
